title: Introducing the SpiceDB Playground Assistant
summary: We've added an AI assistant to the SpiceDB Playground. It writes and edits your schema, generates relationship data and assertions to test it, runs permission checks, and explains exactly why a check was granted or denied.
body_text: We've added an AI assistant to the SpiceDB Playground, and the short version is: it gets you from an idea to a working, tested permission model faster. It writes and edits your schema, generates relationship data and assertions to test it, runs permission checks, and can explain exactly why a check was granted or denied — all from a normal conversation, without leaving the browser. The Playground has always been the easiest way to try SpiceDB: nothing to install, a real build of SpiceDB running via WebAssembly, and enough example schemas for inspiration before you write your own. The Assistant builds on that: learning and iterating on a permissions model now feels less like reading documentation and more like asking someone who's done it before. Asking the Assistant to draft a schema from a plain-language description. What the Assistant does for you Learn. You're new to SpiceDB and have an idea for a permissions model but don't know where to start. You can ask the Assistant to write a first draft, or just ask it questions: what a relation is, how this differs from plain role-based access control, why a pattern exists the way it does. More approachable than having to search through the docs. Build. You want to extend an example schema. Describe the change you want and the Assistant makes it: schema edits, matching relationship data, and assertions that check the change actually does what you asked for. It validates its own edits before applying them. You get something tested, not a snippet you still have to wire up yourself. Understand. You run a permission check but don't understand the result. Ask why it came out that way. The Assistant pulls the real trace and tells you which path in the relationship graph produced the result. Ask to add more test data if you want to dig into it further. Iterate. You have an idea for optimizing your schema. You can prompt the Assistant to implement it. The Assistant keeps a revision history for the session, so you can revert to any earlier point and try a different direction if your idea didn't quite work. Makes it cheap to just try things and see what happens. Selecting Ask assistant to fix on a validation error to have the Assistant repair it automatically. Everything it can do (with prompts to try) Schema and relationship data Write a schema from a plain-language description of your permissions model Add, remove, or modify relations and permissions in an existing schema Generate example relationship data that matches your schema Generate or update assertions and expected-relations tests Checks and validation Run a permission check and report the result Run schema and relationship validation Ask the Assistant to fix a schema error Explain a check with the full debug trace — which path in the relationship graph was traversed for the result Revision history Keep a revision history across the session Revert the schema, relationships, or assertions to any earlier point Reference Ask questions about the schema language and ReBAC concepts Get a best-practice tip on request A few prompts worth copy-pasting in to try it yourself: Write a schema for a project management tool with owners, admins, and members. Add a "commenter" role that can view and comment on tasks but not edit. Add test relationships for a project moonshot Why is alice denied view access on project:moonshot? Generate more test relationships to cover the admin role. Revert to the version before adding the commenter role. What's a common mistake people make modeling multi-tenant permissions? Give me a random schema design tip. Playground as an entry point None of this is a simulation. The Playground runs an actual build of SpiceDB and the zed CLI, compiled to WebAssembly, so the checks and validation you run give you the same answers a production cluster would. That's always been true of the Playground and it's why what you build there is actually usable afterward. When you're ready, AuthZed Cloud gets you a hosted SpiceDB instance to run that same schema in a few minutes. AI tools for SpiceDB The Assistant is built on spicedb-dev , a plugin we maintain for coding agents. In the Playground it's scoped to your browser session, but the plugin itself is a more capable, end-to-end tool that integrates directly with Claude Code or Codex. When you're ready to move from designing a schema to integrating it into a real application, the plugin can work with your coding agent in your own codebase. Try the Assistant now at play.authzed.com , and find spicedb-dev in the authzed-marketplace when you're ready to go further. title: Townsquare Announces Conference Call to Discuss Second Quarter 2026 Results
summary: Townsquare Media, Inc. (NYSE: TSQ) announced today that it will release second quarter 2026 financial results before the market opens on Thursday, August 6, 2026. ...
body_text: Purchase, NY – July 15, 2026 – Townsquare Media, Inc. (NYSE: TSQ) (“Townsquare” or the “Company”) announced today that it will release second quarter 2026 financial results before the market opens on Thursday, August 6, 2026. The Company will host a conference call to discuss certain second quarter 2026 financial results on Thursday, August 6, 2026 at 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time. The conference call dial-in number is 1-800-717-1738 (U.S. & Canada) or 1-646-307-1865 (International) and the conference ID is “Townsquare.” A live webcast of the conference call as well as the press release disclosing the Company’s results will be available on the investor relations page of the Company’s website at www.townsquaremedia.com . A telephone replay of the conference call will be available through August 13, 2026. To access the replay, please dial 1-844-512-2921 (U.S. & Canada) or 1-412-317-6671 (International) and enter confirmation code 1196403. A web-based archive of the conference call will also be available on the investor relations page of the Company’s website. About Townsquare Media, Inc. Townsquare is a community-focused digital and broadcast media and digital marketing solutions company principally focused outside the top 50 markets in the U.S. Townsquare Ignite , our robust digital advertising division, specializes in helping businesses of all sizes connect with their target audience through data-driven, results based strategies, by utilizing a) our proprietary digital programmatic advertising technology stack with an in-house demand and data management platform and b) our owned and operated portfolio of more than 400 local news and entertainment websites and mobile apps along with a network of leading national music and entertainment brands, collecting valuable first party data. Townsquare Interactive , our subscription digital marketing services business, partners with SMBs to help manage their digital presence by providing a SAAS business management platform, website design, creation and hosting, search engine optimization and other digital services. And through our portfolio of local radio stations strategically situated outside the Top 50 markets in the United States, we provide effective advertising solutions for our clients and relevant local content for our audiences. For more information, please visit www.townsquaremedia.com , www.townsquareinteractive.com , and www.townsquareignite.com . title: Olaplex guide to changing hair types: what age, hormones, and damage d
summary: Yes, a person’s hair type can change over time. The sharper answer: what changes may be your curl behavior, strand thickness, density, oiliness, dryness, frizz.
body_text: Yes, a person’s hair type can change over time. The sharper answer: what changes may be your curl behavior, strand thickness, density, oiliness, dryness, frizz, breakage, or the way your lengths hold shape—not always one neat switch from one “type” to another. Hair quality and type can change with time, and aging hair changes can be influenced by factors such as environment, general health, hormones, inflammation, genetics, grooming habits, stress, smoking, and diet.[10] That distinction matters. A new wave pattern at the roots calls for a different read than straight, frayed ends after years of heat styling. OLAPLEX looks at the foundation first: what is happening to the hair fiber, where the change starts, and how your routine can support the hair you have now. What “Hair Type Change” Can Actually Mean When people say their hair type changed, they may be talking about several different traits at once: What changed? What it may point to New curls, waves, or straighter roots A shift connected to follicle behavior, age, hormones, or life stage Hair feels finer or less dense Changes in strand diameter, hair density, growth cycle, or breakage Hair feels coarse, dry, or less silky Lower oil production, dryness, damage, or buildup Curls look frizzy or less defined Damage, dryness, friction, split ends, or styling routine mismatch Ends look thin, see-through, or uneven Breakage, heat, chemical services, rough detangling, or long-term wear Hair type and curl pattern are closely tied to follicle shape, and follicle shape can shift slightly as follicles change with age.[10] At the same time, scientific reviews describe hair as dynamic across life stages, with changes in diameter and pigmentation from childhood through puberty, adulthood, and older age.[5] In plain language: your hair is not frozen in time. Neither is your routine. The Quick Diagnosis: Check New Growth Versus Ends Start with the simplest mirror test: compare your new growth to your mid-lengths and ends. If the change starts at the roots Changes in new growth can suggest that the hair being produced now is different from the hair produced years ago. That can happen as follicles, strand diameter, oil production, density, or the hair cycle change over time. Hair type and texture can also be influenced by hormones, general health, and life stage, so the roots can tell a useful story.[10] Look for cues like: New waves or curls at the root while older lengths still hang straighter. Finer-feeling new growth compared with older hair. Less volume at the scalp that feels different from simple product buildup. Drier roots or scalp changes that affect how hair behaves from the start. If the change mostly shows up on the lengths and ends Changes concentrated from mid-lengths down often point to the hair shaft—the part of hair that has already grown out and lived through brushing, heat, color, sun, friction, and styling. Damaged hair is more fragile and tends to break, which can leave hair looking frizzy and less healthy.[8] Look for cues like: Curls that spring at the roots but fall flat at the ends. A rough or straw-like feel after heat styling, bleaching, coloring, or chemical services. Frizz that appears even when the weather is calm. Split ends, snapping, dullness, or uneven density at the perimeter. Fine hair may show damage as limpness or flyaways. Thick hair may show it as bulk without definition. Curly and coily hair may show it as dryness, tangles, frizz, or stretched-out ends. Straight and wavy hair may show it as dullness, roughness, or a shape that no longer falls cleanly. The goal is not to force your hair into an old category. It is to read what it is asking for now. Why Age And Hormones Can Make Hair Feel Different Aging can change more than hair color. A scientific review of hair aging notes changes in growth, pigmentation, sebum production, fiber diameter, and density.[4] Another review notes that anagen—the active growth phase—can become shorter with aging, more hairs can remain in the resting phase, and hair density can decline with age.[5] That can translate into changes you can feel and see: Hair may feel finer. Individual strand diameter can decline with age, making hair feel less thick and more prone to damage.[10] Hair may feel drier or coarser. Aging follicles can produce less sebum, the natural oil that helps keep hair from feeling dry and brittle.[10] Hair may look less dense. Density changes can make a once-full shape feel lighter or less voluminous.[5] Hair may reflect light differently. Changes in pigment, graying, dryness, and surface condition can affect shine and softness.[4] Hormones can also play a role, but this is where precision matters. Menopause and related hormone-level changes can affect the hair cycle and common hair conditions.[6] The American Academy of Dermatology also notes that menopause can bring noticeable hair changes as hormone levels fall.[7] Some research suggests estrogen is involved in hair growth, with hair diameter changes observed around pregnancy and the perimenopausal transition, but that should be framed carefully—not as a guarantee that hormones will change everyone’s curl pattern.[5] So, can hormones change hair texture? They may contribute to changes in hair amount, growth behavior, dryness, and perceived texture. But a texture change alone does not diagnose a hormone issue, and products should not be framed as changing hormones, genetics, or follicle biology. If you are concerned about thinning or hair loss, or your routine changes are not helping, seeing a dermatologist is recommended.[8] How Damage Can Mimic A New Hair Type Damage can make hair act like it has become a different type because damage changes the condition of the hair shaft. Hair that used to curl may look limp at the ends. Hair that used to feel smooth may feel rough. Thick hair may feel puffy instead of polished. Fine hair may seem even finer because breakage removes length and density. Common damage triggers include: Frequent heat styling or high heat settings. Bleach, color, relaxers, perms, or other chemical services. UV and environmental exposure. Friction from towels, pillows, hats, or tight hairstyles. Rough brushing, detangling, or stretching when hair is vulnerable. Excessive heat can damage hair regardless of hair type, so limiting blow-drying and hot tools and using lower settings is a smart routine move.[9] If damaging practices continue, hair may eventually appear thinner or develop more serious breakage patterns.[8] Where OLAPLEX Fits When Damage Is The Issue If your change is mainly damage-driven—roughness, frizz, breakage, split ends, weakness, or less definition through the lengths—repair care belongs in the conversation. N°.3PLUS Complete Repair Treatment is a 3-minute, protein-free pre-shampoo treatment that uses patented OLAPLEX Bond Building Technology™ and a Damage Defense Cationic Complex to repair all three hair bonds from cortex to cuticle, delivering softer, stronger hair and defending against future damage for all hair types.[1] That makes it a focused option when the hair fiber needs support. N°.3PLUS also works on all hair types, textures, and all types of damage.[1] The important boundary: it is not a way to change your natural hair type, follicle shape, genetics, hormones, or age-related biology. Think repair and resilience—not rewriting your roots. What To Do Next: Build A Routine For The Hair You Have Now The strongest routine is not the one you used five years ago. It is the one that matches your current hair behavior. Start here: Choose care for your current hair type and texture. Dermatology guidance recommends choosing hair-care products made for your hair type, whether curly, straight, coarse, fine, or another type.[9] Wash based on scalp oil and buildup. Wash frequency should depend on how oily or dirty hair gets; dry, textured, curly, or thick hair may need less frequent shampooing than straight or oily hair.[9] Focus shampoo on the scalp. Cleansing the scalp helps remove buildup and excess oil without over-drying the lengths.[9] Condition consistently. Conditioner after every shampoo is a dermatologist-recommended change to help prevent damage.[8] Lower the heat load. Limit hot tools where possible, use lower settings, and avoid stacking heat on already fragile ends.[9] Handle hair like fabric you want to keep. Detangle gently, reduce friction, avoid tight repeat styling, and be strategic with chemical services. For medium-to-coarse hair that needs wash-care support, Olaplex Nº.4 Bond Maintenance Shampoo is formulated for straight, wavy, curly, and coily hair types with medium-to-coarse textures and all porosity levels.[2] It gently cleanses without stripping essential moisture, repairs everyday damage, strengthens and reinforces bonds, replenishes hydration, enhances softness, and is proven to boost shine, smooth hair, and reduce frizz.[2] If damage is making your hair feel weaker, rougher, frizzier, or less like itself, support the hair you have now: explore N°.3PLUS for focused repair care, and consider Nº.4 if medium-to-coarse wash care fits your current texture and routine. FAQ Can Straight Hair Become Curly Or Curly Hair Become Straighter Over Time? Yes, some people notice curl-behavior changes over time. Hair type and curl pattern are connected to follicle shape, and follicle changes with age can slightly affect that shape.[10] But not every curl change starts at the follicle. If new growth is curling differently, age, hormones, or life stage may be part of the picture. If only the ends look straighter, frizzier, or less defined, damage is a more likely suspect. Can Hormones Change Hair Texture? Hormone shifts can contribute to changes in the hair cycle, hair amount, dryness, and perceived texture. Menopause and related hormone changes have been associated with effects on the hair cycle and common hair conditions.[6] Still, hormones should not be treated as a guaranteed explanation for curl-pattern changes. If hair changes are sudden, heavy shedding appears, or thinning concerns you, a dermatologist can help identify what is really happening.[8] Can Damaged Hair Look Like A Different Hair Type? Yes. Damage can make hair look and feel like a different type because it affects the hair shaft. Fragile hair tends to break, and breakage can create frizz and an unhealthy-looking finish.[8] Curly hair may lose definition. Fine hair may look thinner. Thick hair may feel rougher or puffier. Straight or wavy hair may look dull, uneven, or harder to smooth. Can Products Change My Natural Hair Type? No cosmetic product should be framed as changing your genetics, follicle shape, hormones, or natural hair type. Products can support the condition of the hair fiber—strength, softness, hydration, shine, smoothness, manageability, and damage repair—within their supported claims. That is the smart line: care can help hair look and feel better, but it does not rewrite the biology that creates new growth. The Bottom Line Hair can change over time, and the reason is not always one thing. Age can affect growth, pigment, density, oil production, and strand diameter.[4] Hormone shifts may influence hair cycles and perceived texture.[6] Damage can make the lengths look frizzy, weak, dull, broken, or less defined.[8] Your best first move is simple and powerful: check whether the change starts at the roots or lives mostly on the ends, then build a routine for the hair in front of you. Sources [1] Olaplex N°.3PLUS Complete Repair Treatment [2] Olaplex No.4 Bond Maintenance Shampoo, Travel 100ml [4] Hair Aging and Hair Disorders in Elderly Patients [5] Hair Aging in Different Races and Ethnicities [6] Menopause, skin and common dermatoses. Part 1: hair disorders | PubMed [7] Caring for your skin in menopause | American Academy of Dermatology [8] How to stop damaging your hair | American Academy of Dermatology [9] Tips for healthy hair | American Academy of Dermatology [10] Your guide to aging and hair | UCLA Health

title: Swimmer’s Ear: Symptoms, Treatment and Prevention
summary: Everything you need to know about swimmer's ear. Causes and common symptoms as well as home remedies and treatment. Advice for preventing ear infection.
body_text: From beach days to pool parties, with warm weather comes the joy of water activities. Along with sunshine and splash time comes the risk of developing a common and uncomfortable condition: swimmer’s ear. Known medically as otitis externa , swimmer’s ear is an outer ear infection that thrives in warm, moist environments. It may begin with a slight itch or a sensation of fullness in your ear. But if left untreated, it can quickly become painful, disruptive, and even dangerous. If you spend time swimming, sweating, or showering this season, it’s worth understanding what causes swimmer’s ear, how to recognize it early, and how to keep it from cutting your summer short. What is swimmer’s ear? Swimmer’s ear affects the external auditory canal. This narrow passage connects the visible part of your ear to your eardrum. The skin inside this canal is thin, delicate, and protected by a natural acidic film of wax called cerumen. This barrier prevents bacteria and fungi from entering under normal circumstances. The trouble starts when moisture, irritation, or damage disrupts this natural protection. Water that stays trapped in the ear canal can soften the skin and alter the pH level, making it easier for bacteria or fungi to grow. That’s why swimmer’s ear is more likely to happen during summer or in people who spend a lot of time in the water. But you don’t have to be an athlete or a frequent swimmer to be at risk. The condition can also develop from skin conditions, cleaning practices, or the use of earbuds or hearing aids. Is swimmer’s ear a type of ear infection? Yes, swimmer’s ear is a type of ear infection, but it is different from the middle ear infections most people are familiar with. Understanding how these two conditions differ can help you recognize symptoms early and choose the right course of care. Swimmer’s ear vs. middle ear infection Swimmer’s ear is an infection of the outer ear canal. This is the narrow passage that runs from the outside of your ear to the eardrum. The infection typically develops when moisture becomes trapped in the canal, creating the perfect conditions for bacteria or fungi to grow. It can also result from skin irritation, allergic reactions, or tiny abrasions caused by cleaning the ears too aggressively. In contrast, middle ear infections, known as otitis media , occur in the air-filled space behind the eardrum. These infections often follow a cold, sinus congestion, or respiratory illness. When fluid builds up inside the middle ear, it can become infected and painful, especially in young children. Middle ear infections tend to be associated with fever, irritability, and pressure behind the eardrum, while swimmer’s ear is more likely to cause pain when the outer ear is touched. Although both are considered ear infections, they affect different parts of the ear and require different types of treatment. What causes swimmer’s ear? The most common cause of swimmer’s ear is trapped water in the outer ear canal. But that’s just one piece of the puzzle. The real problem is when the combination of moisture and damage allows harmful microorganisms to multiply. Here are the most frequent causes of swimmer’s ear: Prolonged moisture exposure from swimming, bathing, or sweating Tiny abrasions from cotton swabs, fingernails, earbuds, or hearing aids Skin irritation from hair sprays, dyes, or excessive chlorine exposure Underlying conditions like eczema, psoriasis, or seborrheic dermatitis Excessive ear cleaning that strips away protective earwax Narrow ear canals that hold onto moisture more easily Certain bacteria, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus , are common culprits in bacterial swimmer’s ear. In some cases, fungal infections may also be responsible, particularly after prolonged use of antibiotics or exposure to contaminated water. Who is at risk for developing swimmer’s ear? Swimmer’s ear can affect people of all ages, but certain individuals are more likely to develop it due to factors such as behavior, anatomy, or underlying health conditions. By understanding your personal risk factors, you can take steps to protect your ears and reduce the likelihood of infection, especially during the warmer months. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), approximately 2.4 million U.S. healthcare visits occur each year related to swimmer’s ear. While both children and adults are affected, the condition is most common in children between the ages of 7 and 14, particularly those who swim regularly. However, adults are also at risk. Anyone exposed to water, humidity, or frequent skin irritation may develop swimmers’ ear if proper precautions are not taken. The most common risk factors include: Frequent swimming or water exposure Regular swimming, especially in pools, lakes, or oceans, increases the likelihood of water becoming trapped in the ear canal. Children and teens involved in swim teams or water sports are especially vulnerable during summer. Even frequent showering or bathing can pose a risk if water is not properly drained. Use of ear-cleaning tools or devices Inserting cotton swabs, bobby pins, or other objects into the ear canal can cause tiny abrasions. These small injuries allow bacteria or fungi to enter and take hold. Over-cleaning can also strip away protective earwax, which normally serves as a barrier against infection. Earbud or hearing aid use Wearing in-ear devices for long periods creates a warm, moist environment that supports microbial growth. Earbuds may also irritate the skin inside the canal or introduce bacteria if not kept clean. Narrow or curved ear canals Some individuals naturally have ear canals that are narrower or more curved in shape. This anatomical feature makes it more difficult for water to drain, increasing the likelihood that moisture will remain trapped inside the ear. Skin conditions affecting the ear canal Individuals with eczema, psoriasis, or seborrheic dermatitis are more susceptible to skin inflammation and cracking. These disruptions weaken the ear’s natural defenses, making it easier for bacteria and fungi to cause infection. Allergies or sensitivities to hair and skin products Hairsprays, shampoos, and other cosmetic products can enter the ear canal and irritate its lining. Over time, repeated exposure may cause chronic inflammation or disrupt the balance of healthy bacteria. Age and activity level Children between the ages of 7 and 14 are the most commonly affected, particularly during the summer. However, active adults who engage in swimming, surfing, or outdoor sports in hot or humid conditions are also at risk. Sweat, heat, and high humidity all increase moisture in and around the ear canal. Weakened immune system or chronic illness People with conditions that affect immune function, such as diabetes, cancer, or autoimmune disorders, have a higher risk of developing severe or recurring infections. In these cases, swimmer’s ear may require more aggressive treatment and should be monitored closely by a healthcare provider. While swimmer’s ear can affect anyone, certain individuals are more likely to develop it due to their habits, environment, or health status. Children and teens who swim regularly, adults who frequently use earbuds or hearing aids, and individuals with skin conditions or compromised immune systems face a higher risk. Understanding these risk factors and making small changes, such as thoroughly drying your ears, avoiding irritation, and protecting the ear canal, can reduce your chances of infection and help you stay comfortable throughout the season. What are the common symptoms of swimmer’s ear? Swimmer’s ear symptoms usually develop within a few days of exposure. The infection often begins with mild discomfort or itching, but can progress quickly if left untreated. Common symptoms include: Itching inside the ear canal Pain that worsens when the ear is pulled or touched Redness and visible swelling of the outer ear A sense of fullness or pressure inside the ear Drainage from the ear, which may be clear, yellow, or pus-like Muffled or reduced hearing on the affected side Swollen lymph nodes near the jaw or neck Low-grade fever in more advanced infections In severe cases, pain may radiate into the face, neck, or head. If the infection spreads beyond the ear canal, it may cause systemic symptoms and requires immediate medical care. If you notice these symptoms, especially if the pain is increasing or drainage persists, it is essential to seek care promptly. Prompt treatment can reduce discomfort and prevent complications. Is swimmer’s ear serious? Swimmer’s ear is usually mild when caught early, but it should never be ignored. Without treatment, the infection can worsen and lead to more significant health issues. Potential complications include: Persistent pain and inflammation that interferes with sleep or daily activities Temporary hearing loss caused by swelling or fluid in the canal Recurring infections that lead to thickened skin and narrowed canals Chronic otitis externa, where the infection lingers for weeks or returns frequently Cellulitis, a bacterial skin infection that can spread to surrounding areas Malignant otitis externa is a rare but life-threatening condition in which the infection spreads to the bones of the skull. This occurs most often in people with diabetes, weakened immune systems, or chronic illness. Even if the infection stays local, it can be disruptive. Children may miss camp, sports, or swimming lessons. Adults may struggle with work, sleep, or using headphones. If left unaddressed, what starts as a small issue can take a significant toll. When to seek medical care for swimmer’s ear Not every case of swimmer’s ear requires medical treatment, especially if symptoms are caught early and managed appropriately at home. However, when the condition progresses, becomes more painful, or fails to improve within a few days, professional care is essential. Even mild outer ear infections can worsen if left untreated. In some cases, the infection may spread beyond the ear canal or lead to long-term complications that affect hearing, comfort, or skin health. Warning signs that require medical attention include: Symptoms lasting longer than 48 hours , especially if they show no signs of improvement Pain that intensifies or begins to radiate into the face, jaw, or neck Visible drainage from the ear, especially if it is yellow, green, foul-smelling, or persistent Noticeable swelling or redness of the outer ear or surrounding skin Muffled or reduced hearing , which may indicate swelling or fluid blockage inside the canal Fever , chills, or signs of systemic infection Chronic conditions such as diabetes, autoimmune disorders, or immunosuppression, which can increase the risk of complications Prompt diagnosis not only relieves symptoms more quickly but also prevents the infection from becoming more severe or difficult to treat. Early intervention is especially important for children, older adults, and anyone with underlying health concerns. How is swimmer’s ear diagnosed? If you visit a healthcare provider with symptoms of swimmer’s ear, the diagnostic process usually begins with a detailed clinical exam. This enables the provider to confirm the diagnosis, identify potential complications, and tailor the treatment plan to your unique symptoms and medical history. During the exam, the provider may: Use an otoscope to visually examine the ear canal and eardrum Look for signs of redness, swelling, flaking skin, or visible discharge Gently manipulate the outer ear to assess pain and tenderness Ask about recent water exposure, ear cleaning habits, or use of earbuds or hearing aids In some cases, a sample of fluid or debris from the ear canal may be collected and tested in a lab to determine whether the infection is caused by bacteria or fungi. Identifying the exact organism helps ensure that the prescribed treatment is appropriate and effective. If the infection is unusually severe, recurring, or unresponsive to treatment, the provider may recommend additional imaging, such as a CT scan, to rule out deeper infections or structural issues. This step is more common in high-risk individuals or when symptoms extend beyond the ear. By combining a physical exam with a patient’s history and symptom progression, healthcare providers can accurately diagnose swimmer’s ear and prescribe treatment that relieves symptoms and prevents future infections. How is swimmer’s ear treated? The treatment approach for swimmer’s ear depends on how far the infection has progressed, what caused it, and how your body is responding to it. In its early stages, swimmer’s ear may be managed with basic home care. When symptoms become more advanced or persistent, professional medical treatment is necessary to fully resolve the infection and prevent complications. Home treatment options for mild swimmer’s ear For mild symptoms, the goal is to stop the infection from progressing while relieving discomfort. If the infection is caught early and symptoms are limited to mild itching or a sense of fullness in the ear, self-care at home may be enough to resolve the issue. Recommended home care includes: Keeping the ear dry at all times. Avoid swimming or exposing the ear to water while symptoms are present. Use a shower cap or earplugs if needed. Using over-the-counter drying drops , especially after swimming or bathing. These solutions, which often contain isopropyl alcohol and acetic acid, help remove moisture and maintain the ear canal’s natural protective acidity. Taking oral pain relievers , such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen. These can help manage discomfort and reduce inflammation. Applying a warm compress , such as a clean washcloth soaked in warm (not hot) water and wrung out, then placed against the outer ear. The warmth may help ease localized pain or tension around the ear and jaw. Resting on the opposite side to promote natural drainage and reduce pressure. If your right ear is affected, lying on your left side may encourage gravity to assist in fluid movement and relieve pressure. While these steps may resolve early symptoms, it’s important to monitor for any signs of worsening. If symptoms persist longer than two days, become more painful, or involve discharge, professional evaluation is recommended. Medical treatment for moderate to severe infections When swimmer’s ear progresses beyond the mild stage, medical intervention is typically required. A healthcare provider will evaluate the ear canal and determine the type and extent of the infection. Treatment usually involves ear drops that target the source of infection and reduce inflammation. Common prescriptions include: Antibiotic ear drops are used to treat the infection by killing the bacteria that cause it. These often contain medications like ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin, which are effective against common bacterial strains found in outer ear infections. Steroid ear drops help calm the body’s inflammatory response. Swelling, redness, and pain may decrease more rapidly with the addition of corticosteroids. Antifungal ear drops are prescribed when a fungus rather than bacteria causes the infection. Fungal infections are less common but may occur after prolonged exposure to moisture or repeated use of antibiotic drops. Additional medical procedures for treating swimmer’s ear In more severe cases, the ear canal may be too swollen or obstructed for ear drops to work effectively. To improve medication delivery and reduce symptoms, a provider may need to: Gently clean the ear canal using specialized tools and techniques. This procedure removes debris, wax buildup, or discharge that may be blocking the canal or harboring bacteria. Insert a medicated wick into the ear canal. This small, soft piece of material absorbs the prescribed drops and helps carry the medication deeper into the swollen canal. The wick may stay in place for 24 to 72 hours and is removed or replaced as needed during follow-up care. When oral antibiotics are prescribed If the infection has spread beyond the ear canal or if topical treatment fails to resolve symptoms, oral antibiotics may be prescribed. These are usually reserved for cases where: There is visible swelling around the outer ear or face Lymph nodes in the neck are inflamed The patient has a fever or signs of systemic infection The patient has a chronic illness or a compromised immune system Oral medications provide systemic support, reaching areas that topical treatments cannot. Your provider will select the most suitable antibiotic based on the suspected bacteria and your individual health profile. Recovery timeline and follow-up With proper treatment, most people begin to feel better within 48 to 72 hours. Pain, swelling, and discharge usually improve first, followed by a gradual return to normal hearing and comfort. However, the length of recovery can vary depending on how early the infection was treated and whether there are any underlying risk factors, such as skin conditions or diabetes. It’s important to: Complete the full course of prescribed medication , even if symptoms improve quickly. Stopping treatment early can allow bacteria to return or become resistant. Keep the ear dry throughout treatment and recovery , using shower caps or earplugs to protect against additional moisture. Avoid inserting anything into the ear , including fingers, cotton swabs, or earbuds, until the ear has fully healed. Your provider may schedule a follow-up visit to assess healing and ensure that the infection has fully resolved. If symptoms recur or do not improve, further testing may be needed to rule out a fungal infection, resistant bacteria, or a chronic skin condition affecting the ear canal. Can chiropractic help with swimmer’s ear? While research is limited, many patients report improvement in symptoms related to middle ear infections while receiving chiropractic care. These benefits are believed to result from improved nervous system function, enhanced fluid drainage, and reduced inflammation in the vicinity of the auditory canal. When spinal alignment supports clearer communication between the brain and body, it may also support the natural mechanisms that help regulate pressure and drainage in the ear. In swimmer’s ear, the infection begins in the outer ear canal and is usually triggered by trapped moisture, skin irritation, or bacterial exposure. Because this condition results from local environmental factors rather than internal congestion, chiropractic care is not used to treat swimmer’s ear directly. However, chiropractic care may still support the body’s natural ability to recover from infections by promoting a properly functioning nervous system, which may help reduce inflammation. That said, people who experience frequent ear infections, tension in the jaw or neck, or reduced lymphatic drainage may benefit from chiropractic care as part of a broader wellness routine. A licensed chiropractor can evaluate your spine and nervous system and recommend a care plan tailored to your individual needs. Expert tips for preventing swimmer’s ear The best way to manage swimmer’s ear is to prevent it from occurring in the first place. With a few consistent habits, you can keep your ears healthy all season long. Here’s how to protect yourself or your kiddos from swimmer’s ear: Keep your ears dry: After swimming or showering, tilt your head to help water drain from your ears. Gently dry the outer ear with a towel. Avoid inserting anything into the canal. Use a hairdryer: Set it on the lowest setting and hold it at least 12 inches from your ear. This helps evaporate moisture that may have become trapped. Wear ear protection in the water: Use waterproof earplugs or a swim cap to prevent water from entering your ears, especially if you’re prone to infections. Avoid contaminated water: Don’t swim in lakes, rivers, or poorly maintained pools. These environments may contain bacteria or fungi that increase your risk of infection. Don’t use cotton swabs: Resist the urge to clean your ears with swabs, bobby pins, or fingers. These items can scratch the skin and push wax deeper into the ear. Use ear drops preventively: If you’re prone to swimmer’s ear, ask your provider about using over-the-counter drops made with acetic acid or alcohol to maintain a healthy pH in your ear canal. Manage skin conditions: If you have eczema or psoriasis, follow your provider’s guidance for care. These conditions can make the ear canal more vulnerable to infection. Monitor for early symptoms: Be aware of itching, fullness, or mild discomfort. Treating symptoms early can help prevent the infection from becoming serious. Keep your ears healthy all summer long Swimmer’s ear may seem like a seasonal inconvenience, but it can quickly become a more serious issue if left untreated. The good news is that it is one of the most preventable summer health concerns. Taking a little care after swimming, packing a few protective tools in your pool bag, and understanding what your ears need can help keep you comfortable, active, and enjoying every moment. From diving boards to beach waves, your ears play a bigger role in your health than you may realize. Pay attention to how they feel. Keep them clean, dry, and protected. And take early signs seriously. Your ears will thank you with clarity, comfort, and full participation in everything summer brings The information, including but not limited to text, graphics, images, and other material contained on this page, is for informational purposes only. title: aTyr Pharma to Present Subgroup Analysis of Phase 3 EFZO-FIT™ Study of Efzofitimod in Pulmonary Sarcoidosis at WASOG 2026
summary: Patients with restrictive lung disease demonstrate clinically meaningful benefit in FVC and improvements in multiple PROs for 5.0 mg/kg efzofitimod compared to placebo. Company submitted protocol to FDA in June 2026 for planned Phase 3 study of efzofitimod in patients with chronic, symptomatic
body_text: aTyr Pharma to Present Subgroup Analysis of Phase 3 EFZO-FIT™ Study of Efzofitimod in Pulmonary Sarcoidosis at WASOG 2026 PDF Version Jul 15, 2026 Patients with restrictive lung disease demonstrate clinically meaningful benefit in FVC and improvements in multiple PROs for 5.0 mg/kg efzofitimod compared to placebo. Company submitted protocol to FDA in June 2026 for planned Phase 3 study of efzofitimod in patients with chronic, symptomatic pulmonary sarcoidosis with restrictive lung disease. SAN DIEGO, July 15, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- aTyr Pharma, Inc. (Nasdaq: ATYR) (“aTyr” or the “Company”), a clinical stage biotechnology company engaged in the discovery and development of first-in-class medicines from its proprietary tRNA synthetase platform, today announced that the Company will present a subgroup analysis of the Phase 3 EFZO-FIT™ study of efzofitimod in pulmonary sarcoidosis, a major form of interstitial lung disease, at the World Association of Sarcoidosis and Other Granulomatous Disorders (WASOG) 2026 Congress, which is scheduled to take place July 15 – 17, 2026, in Porto, Portugal. “This subgroup analysis of patients from EFZO-FIT™ with restrictive lung disease presents clear evidence that those treated with efzofitimod experienced a clinically meaningful benefit in lung function and positive trends of improvement in multiple patient-reported outcomes (PROs) while removing steroids,” said Sanjay S. Shukla, M.D., M.S., President and Chief Executive Officer of aTyr Pharma. “Following our recent interactions with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), last month we submitted a protocol for a planned Phase 3 study in pulmonary sarcoidosis patients with restrictive lung disease (defined as forced vital capacity, or FVC, percent predicted ≤ 80% with a normal FEV1/FVC ratio), utilizing FVC as the primary endpoint of the study and the King’s Sarcoidosis Questionnaire (KSQ)-Lung score as the key secondary endpoint. We believe the approach of investigating efzofitimod in this defined patient population where FVC is the relevant measure of lung function is a well-informed plan to demonstrate the potential for efzofitimod to improve the lives of these patients.” Details of the poster presentation appear below. The poster will be available on the aTyr website once presented. Title: Evaluating Efzofitimod in a Subset of Sarcoidosis with the Restrictive Phenotype Authors: Vis Niranjan, Pavithra Ramesh, Sanjay Shukla, Nelson Kinnersley, Daniel A. Culver. RxMD, aTyr Pharma, Octa Consulting Services, Cleveland Clinic. Poster Number: PO123 Session: Controversies in Sarcoidosis Treatment and Disease Progression Date and Time: Thursday, July 16, 2026, at 1:15pm WEST Location: Porto, Portugal EFZO-FIT™ included 264 pulmonary sarcoidosis patients with all lung phenotypes who were enrolled and treated (intent-to-treat, or ITT). The post hoc analysis included a subset of 44 patients with prespecified restrictive lung disease (FVCpp ≤ 80%, FEV1/FVC ≥ 0.7). The change from baseline at week 48 for FVC and PROs was analyzed using a random coefficient regression model (RCRM) to supplement the mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) analysis performed for the ITT data. The baseline characteristics were generally balanced in the restrictive patients compared to the ITT population, however mean FVC was expectedly lower. Overall, the magnitude of steroid reduction in the 5.0 mg/kg efzofitimod arm was similar to placebo. In the 5.0 mg/kg efzofitimod arm, the placebo adjusted week 48 change from baseline for FVC by RCRM was 123.8 ml. The placebo adjusted week 48 change from baseline by RCRM showed improvement for the 5.0 mg/kg efzofitimod arm versus placebo for KSQ-Lung, KSQ-General Health, Fatigue Assessment Scale, and the Leicester Cough Questionnaire. Furthermore, efzofitimod was generally well tolerated in the restrictive subgroup, similar to the ITT. The findings suggest that further investigation of efzofitimod in patients with restrictive lung disease is warranted. About the EFZO-FIT™ study EFZO-FIT™ was a global Phase 3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of efzofitimod in patients with pulmonary sarcoidosis with all lung phenotypes. The 52-week study consisted of three parallel cohorts randomized equally to either 3.0 mg/kg or 5.0 mg/kg of efzofitimod or placebo dosed intravenously once a month for a total of 12 doses. The study enrolled 268 subjects (264 enrolled and treated) with pulmonary sarcoidosis at multiple centers in the United States, Europe, Japan and Brazil. The trial design incorporated a forced steroid taper. The primary endpoint of the study was steroid reduction at week 48. Secondary endpoints included measures of sarcoidosis symptoms and lung function at week 48. Abo ut Pulmonary Sarcoidosis Pulmonary sarcoidosis is an inflammatory disease characterized by the formulation of granulomas, clumps of inflammatory cells, in one or more organs of the body. Approximately 160,000 Americans are diagnosed with pulmonary sarcoidosis and the prognosis ranges from benign and self-limiting to chronic, debilitating disease, permanent loss of lung function and death. Current treatment options include corticosteroids and other immunosuppressive therapies, which have limited efficacy and are associated with serious side-effects that many patients cannot tolerate long-term. Abo ut Efzofitimod Efzofitimod is a novel biologic immunomodulator in clinical development for the treatment of interstitial lung disease (ILD), a group of immune-mediated disorders that can cause inflammation and fibrosis, or scarring, of the lungs. Efzofitimod is a tRNA synthetase derived therapy that selectively modulates activated myeloid cells through neuropilin-2 to resolve inflammation without immune suppression and potentially prevent the progression of fibrosis. Efzofitimod is currently being investigated in the Phase 2 EFZO-CONNECT™ study in patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc, or scleroderma)-related ILD, and aTyr recently submitted a protocol to the FDA for a global Phase 3 study of efzofitimod in patients with pulmonary sarcoidosis, a major form of ILD. These forms of ILD have limited therapeutic options and there is a need for safer and more effective, disease-modifying treatments that improve outcomes. About aTyr aTyr is a clinical stage biotechnology company leveraging evolutionary intelligence to translate tRNA synthetase biology into new therapies for fibrosis and inflammation. tRNA synthetases are ancient, essential proteins that have evolved novel domains that regulate diverse pathways extracellularly in humans. aTyr’s discovery platform is focused on unlocking hidden therapeutic intervention points by uncovering signaling pathways driven by its proprietary library of domains derived from all 20 tRNA synthetases. aTyr’s lead therapeutic candidate is efzofitimod, a novel biologic immunomodulator in clinical development for the treatment of interstitial lung disease, a group of immune-mediated disorders that can cause inflammation and progressive fibrosis, or scarring, of the lungs. For more information, please visit www.atyrpharma.com . title: FinCEN's Residential Real Estate Reporting Rule Under Section 6403 With AI at the Title and Closing Table: The Nationwide Reporting Person Cascade, the Beneficial-Owner Capture, and What the December 1, 2025 Effective Date Actually Changed
summary: FinCEN's final rule at 31 CFR 1031.320, effective December 1, 2025, replaces the geographic-targeted Real Estate GTO regime with a nationwide reporting obligation on residential-real-estate transfers to legal entities and trusts. The rule uses a reporting-person cascade, requires beneficial-ownership capture on every covered transfer, and imposes a specific 30-day filing window. What the rule actually requires, how the AI agent participates in the closing workflow, and where the compliance risk lands for title, settlement, and mortgage professionals.

title: A Quantitative Systems Pharmacology Comparison Of Tau-targeted Therapeutic Strategies In Alzheimer’s Disease
summary: Certara's quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) model compares tau-targeted therapeutic strategies in Alzheimer's Disease, including antibodies, ASOs, and PTM modifiers, across virtual patient populations stratified by APOE genotype and disease stage.
body_text: Alzheimer’s Disease remains one of the most complex challenges in drug development, with tau pathology playing a central role in neurodegeneration and cognitive decline. Multiple therapeutic strategies are being explored to target tau — but how do they compare, and which holds the greatest promise for meaningful clinical outcomes? In this scientific poster, Certara researchers apply a quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) framework to mechanistically model and compare distinct tau-targeting approaches across virtual patient populations. What You’ll Learn: How QSP modeling can evaluate and differentiate tau-targeted therapeutic strategies, including antibodies, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), and post-translational modification (PTM) modifiers Why spatial accessibility within the synapse may limit the efficacy of anti-tau antibodies despite robust target engagement in CSF How APOE genotype and baseline disease stage influence predicted cognitive response to tau therapy The interplay between amyloid and tau pathology and its implications for treatment timing and patient selection Which intraneuronal tau-targeting mechanisms show the greatest predicted impact on disease biomarkers Why It Matters: Predicting which therapeutic strategy will translate to meaningful clinical benefit in Alzheimer’s Disease is a persistent challenge. This research demonstrates how mechanistic QSP modeling, grounded in real clinical biomarker and outcome data, can generate testable hypotheses, inform trial design, and enable head-to-head comparisons of current and emerging tau therapies. For sponsors developing tau-directed therapies, these insights can support more informed go/no-go decisions and smarter patient population selection. Access this resource

title: King Ranch Is Synonymous with Sun, Snakes, Cattle, and Ford Trucks
summary: It took Robert Silguero a few minutes to find a video on his phone. It shows Silguero, a fifth-generation Kineño as the local cowboys are called, astride his horse out on the range. Suddenly, with a lightning flick of the wrist, he whips his lasso at a movement in the brush and the just-visible tail […]
body_text: It took Robert Silguero a few minutes to find a video on his phone. It shows Silguero, a fifth-generation Kineño as the local cowboys are called, astride his horse out on the range. Suddenly, with a lightning flick of the wrist, he whips his lasso at a movement in the brush and the just-visible tail of a rattler goes limp. “A 7-footer,” he says proudly. Per the local custom, he took the snake and hung it on a fence belly-up as an offering to the rain gods. Amid a withering, months-long drought, King Ranch’s cowboys are willing to do just about anything to undam the heavens. Around these parts, which is about 45 minutes southwest of Corpus Christi, Texas, it’s a rare mile on a highway that you don’t pass half a dozen Ford trucks coming the other way. Some of them bear a chrome “Running W” logo, indicating that they are deluxe King Ranch Editions, an ultra-plus trim level for the Expedition SUV and F-Series pickups. But King Ranch is more than just a Dearborn marketing concoction. It is a real place, situated on a tropical plain abutting the Gulf Coast and paved with oceans of Bermuda and blue-stem grass, cultivated cotton and sorghum fields, sand dunes, watering holes, and dense thickets of gnarled mesquite, prickly agave, and flowering fiddlewood. It is owned by a real family and inhabited by real people and real animals who for generations have eked out a codependent existence under a brutally indifferent sky. Nobody is sure how the ranch came by its Running W logo. One theory is that it’s a tribute to the ranch’s ubiquitous rattlesnakes. The ’49 Ford F-1 may be retired and out to pasture, but it looks ready to jump back into ranch duty at any moment. James Lipman Indeed, the King had been a working ranch for 147 years before Ford came calling in 2000 with an idea to partner up on an F-150 trimmed in saddle leather from the ranch’s sprawling herds. As we discovered in Harrel’s Pharmacy in downtown Kingsville, the relationship goes even further back. Framed on the wall by the lunch counter is a Ford ad from 1949. It reads: “‘With some 50,000 head of cattle on approximately 900,000 acres to look after, the ’49 Ford is a welcome addition to the Ford family. I can drive mine all day without fatigue,’ says Mr. Richard M. Kleberg, Jr. of Kingsville, Texas.” Coincidentally, the vintage Ford F-1 that was brought down from San Antonio by its owner, Hagerty member Ben Sanchez, to be our photo prop, is also from 1949. Its skinny bias-ply tires, rudimentary gauges, and flathead 100-hp V-8 with a three-speed represent accurately what Ford pickups used to be, before they became plush four-door family liners. Back then, pickups were driven almost exclusively by ranchers, farmers, road builders, and other tradespeople needing basic, sturdy workhorses. Computer screens, massaging seats, radar cruise control, and even air conditioning would have all seemed like science-fiction stuff, yet today, a fleet of fuel-injected, semiconductor-stuffed descendants of Sanchez’s ’49 still work the ranch, screens and all. Horses and Ford trucks have been essential equipment at King Ranch for decades. When our ’49 F-1 photo vehicle was new, King Ranch—today the largest ranch in the U.S.—was already 96 years old. James Lipman At 825,000 acres divided into four divisions all in the vicinity of the quiet burg of Kingsville, King Ranch is the largest such ranch in the United States. Vice president and general manager Heath Grigg was quick to apologize for the desiccated state of the landscape when we arrived. “You’re not seeing us at our best,” he said as the relentless sun peeked through early March clouds that offered intermittent shade but no rain. The economics are simple: When it rains, nature provides an abundance of free food in the form of green pastures. When it doesn’t, the ranch has to feed its stock an expensive kibble of protein and grains called “range cubes.” Drought sparks a bitter cycle: As costs go up, the beef supply shrinks, propelling beef prices upward, which eventually causes consumers to look for cheaper alternatives. Especially for the most profitable U.S. Department of Agriculture–rated Prime and Choice varieties that King Ranch prefers to supply. The cowboys like to say that every dry day is “one day closer to rain.” Meanwhile, where 50,000 head of cattle once roamed in fenced pastures that seem to stretch to the horizon, the herd has in recent years been thinned down to about 32,000, mainly of the Santa Cruz and Santa Gertrudis varieties that King Ranch calls its own. Developed through selective breeding, the cattle better endure the high temperatures and humidity of the climate while still producing the beautifully marbled meat that chefs crave. James Lipman Captain Richard King might have picked a more hospitable place for his ranch, but it undoubtedly made sense at the time. Apparently restless as a jewelry apprentice in New York City, King was just 10 when he stole away in 1834 on a steamship bound for Mobile, Alabama. His captain took a shine to him and taught him the ways of the water, and at 21, he joined up to pilot steamers ferrying troops and supplies down the Rio Grande for the Mexican-American War. After the peace, King ran a thriving steamboat business, eventually branching out into land and cattle. He and a partner bought an old 15,500-acre Spanish land grant in 1853 called the Rincón de Santa Gertrudis. The price for this wild land of thickets and snakes was $300 (nobody quite knows the origin of the ranch’s Running W logo, but one theory is that it’s a rattlesnake). A year later, he snapped up another 53,000 acres for $1800, and about 60 other land purchases later, the King Ranch became more or less what it is today. James Lipman James Lipman The Mexican herders who came with their families to work for King called themselves Los Kineños, the King’s People. They formed the wellspring of what today is a community of 300 residents living on the ranch, of whom 160 are employees, many of them multigenerational. Though Captain King had four children, it was only his daughter, Alice Gertrudis King, who bore any children. In 1886, she married Robert Justus Kleberg from a family of locally prominent German immigrants. Thus, while it is still called the King Ranch, it is the Kleberg family who has run it for more than a century. They are the closest thing South Texas has to royalty, which is why you can drive King Avenue through Kingsville out to the gates of King Ranch in Kleberg County. Captain King might have picked a more hospitable place for his ranch. James Lipman The flathead V-8 in the old F-1 burbled lazily as the truck picked its way across one of the ranch’s 32,000-acre pastures, perfectly at home amid the cow patties and dried-up mudholes. Its rudimentary suspension, a half-step up from a prairie schooner’s with its four sets of leaf springs carrying two solid axles, can take plenty of punishment. But the driver on the small, cramped bench feels every impact. The fact that Ford touted this ½-ton truck as having a “Million Dollar Cab” with its “Spiralounge Floating Seat,” “Feather-Foot Braking,” and “Airplane-Style Shocks” seems quaintly hilarious. Sanchez, who admits that he isn’t as svelte as he used to be, installed a small hot rod–style steering wheel just so he could fit behind the wheel. Trucks weren’t large back then and they didn’t weigh nearly as much as they do today. Nor were they able to carry as much. The “Bonus Built” Ford F-1, as Ford called it in the ads, was able to haul 1480 pounds in its bed, for a gross weight rating of 4700 pounds. Today’s bottom basement F-150 with a 2.7- liter turbo V-6 carries 1775 pounds and can tow 8400. Numbers matter on a ranch. So does four-wheel drive, though despite the fact that Ford had built Army jeeps during the war, it would take the company another decade to offer the feature as factory equipment on its pickups. James Lipman The old F-1 was perfectly at home amid the cow patties. Still, the “master of a thousand-and-one light delivery jobs,” as Ford dubbed the new F-1 when it debuted in 1948, had some clever features to help endear it to the ranch hands. As with Ford and Chevy pickups since the ’30s, the sides of the steel cargo box were rolled over into a loop at the top, both to make the bed sides more rigid but also so that items such as sod bags won’t snag but simply slide over into the bed. The bed came standard with holes for stakes, and monotube gas shocks, though not new (wartime jeeps had them), were still novel in 1948. James Lipman James Lipman James Lipman Even so, the most valuable piece of equipment on a ranch in 1948 wasn’t a truck but a horse, a fact we were surprised to learn is still true in 2026. The King Ranch employs 34 cowboys, and the goal is to have four horses for each cowboy to account for rest, feeding, and illness. Between roundups for deworming, vaccination, branding, pasture rotation, shipping to feed lots, and other purposes, the cattle are regularly on the move during their 18-month lives at the ranch. King Ranch runs a clothing boutique in Kingsville that also includes a pro saddle shop. One of the ranch’s cowboys looks on as the broken handgrip horn on his saddle is repaired. James Lipman Why not use cheap dirt bikes or ATVs? “Horses don’t cause fires,” explained Silguero, and they also have brains, which, when tamed and trained, provide the cowboys what in car industry terms might be called Level V self-driving automation. The range is rough, full of mounds and snakes and hidden holes. A horse can pick its way up a trail while the rider looks elsewhere, not possible with a motorized machine. James Lipman Hence the ranch is an American Quarter Horse breeding operation, because it’s cheaper to make at home these compact, agile sprinters than it is to buy them. It costs about $20,000 to $25,000 to breed a horse, what with insemination and vet bills, but that might be half the purchase price of a decent ranch horse. The process is agonizingly slow, however, and not every foal is suitable for range work. A tick-borne disease decimated the ranch’s horse herd 15 years ago and it’s still recovering, said San Antonio veterinarian Ben Espy as he inserted his arm into a mare’s rectum all the way up to his shoulder. Espy, whom the cowboys consider the best equine specialist in the region, was giving the horse an ultrasound. Which, because the 1200-pound animal is so thick, can only be done from the inside, with the probe inserted well up the poop chute. King Ranch maintains its own stock of “recips,” or recipient horses. “They’re professional mothers,” Espy explained, meaning horses whose temperament isn’t suited for anything other than breeding, much of it done through in vitro fertilization. “They’re recips for a reason—they’re a**holes,” he quipped, shortly before one of them kicked her steel stall so hard that it sounded like a gunshot. Head cowboy Lee Roy Montalvo, a seventh-generation Kineño, led four mares into the breeding barn at a time so that Espy could examine their ovaries and see if any had foals aboard. Only one of the mares was pregnant, and Montalvo was disappointed. “This looks easy; it isn’t easy,” he said. It costs $20K to breed a horse, but it’s cheaper than buying. Horses are still the most efficient way to work the ranch, say the cowboys, and it’s cheaper to make good quarter horses than to buy them. The branding barn is where the ranch’s “professional mothers” get their ultrasounds. James Lipman Actually, nothing about working rugged rangeland among thousands of large animals in the South Texas heat looks easy. Silguero, a fifth-generation Kineño who has worked on the ranch since he was 12 and now has two daughters in college, was thrown when he was 17 and lost hearing in one ear. “If you haven’t been bucked off, you’re not riding horses,” he said with a shrug.
